summary: Tipaza, the capital of Algeria’s Tipaza Province, was known as Tipasa under Roman rule; the modern town was founded in 1857 and is a tourist destination chiefly for its ancient ruins and sandy littoral. Originally a Punic trading-post, the settlement became a Roman military colony and Christian hub with three basilicas, underwent destruction and reconstruction, and was settled again in the nineteenth century.

coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: Claudius established Tipasa as a military colony for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauretania; it subsequently became the municipium Colonia Aelia Tipasensis.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The ancient population of 20,000 inhabitants in the fourth century is attributed specifically to Stéphane Gsell; the modern population is described as nearly 30,000 inhabitants.
The modern town founded in 1857 followed ancient destruction, Byzantine reconstruction one century after 430 CE, and demolition at the end of the seventh century.
The transmitter’s reported return to broadcasting at 252 kHz followed an interruption beginning March 17, 2014.

fitAdvice: Tipaza’s ancient ruins are the principal reason identified for its importance as a tourist destination in modern Algeria.
Tipaza and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, described as the largest Berber-speaking group of western Algeria; the majority of the Bouriba family also reside in this area.
The nearby transmitter carries French language Channel 3 programs at 252 kHz, with reception reported in many parts of Europe.
